lead: A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a feedforward network built for grid data such as images. Instead of connecting every input pixel to every unit, it slides a small filter over the image and reuses the same weights at every position. This is convolution. A pooling step then shrinks the map. The two together cut the number of weights by a large factor while keeping local patterns. CNNs are used in face unlock, medical imaging, document scanning and defect detection on factory lines.
prereq: You need: activation functions (ReLU, softmax), backpropagation to see how filters are trained, and deep network basics.

sections.h3: Convolution: a small filter that slides

blocks.text: An image is a grid of numbers: height × width × channels. A dense layer connected to every pixel needs a huge weight matrix. For a 224×224 colour image, one dense layer of 1000 units would need 224×224×3×1000 weights, about 150 million. A convolution layer avoids this by using a small filter, also called a kernel, and sliding it over the grid.

At each position, the filter and the input patch under it are multiplied element by element and summed. That single number becomes one cell of the output map. The patch is the local receptive field of that output cell. The same filter weights are reused at every position; this is weight sharing. A 3×3 filter has 9 weights, not one weight per pixel. In strict signal-processing terms this sliding sum without flipping the filter is cross-correlation; deep-learning libraries call it convolution, and that is the meaning used here.

blocks.where: n is the input side in pixels, p is the padding (extra zero rows and columns on each side), f is the filter side, s is the stride (pixels moved per step), h_out is the output side, and floor means round down to the integer below.

blocks.text: For a 5×5 input, a 3×3 filter, no padding and stride 1: floor((5 + 0 − 3)/1) + 1 = 3, so the output is 3×3. Padding p = 1 on the same input gives floor((5 + 2 − 3)/1) + 1 = 5, so the map keeps the input size. A stride of 2 skips positions and shrinks the map faster.
params = f × f × C_in × K + K
blocks.where: C_in is the number of input channels, K is the number of filters, and the final +K is one bias per filter. For one 3×3 filter on a 1-channel image: 3×3×1×1 + 1 = 10 parameters.

blocks.text: With 3 input channels (red, green, blue) and 16 filters of size 3×3, the count is 3×3×3×16 + 16 = 448. The filter depth must equal C_in; a 3×3 filter on an RGB image is really 3×3×3.

Filter values are learnable weights. Backpropagation adjusts them from the loss, as in any network (see backpropagation). Early filters often become edge or blob detectors. A vertical-edge filter such as rows 1 0 −1 / 1 0 −1 / 1 0 −1 gives a large positive response where the image is bright on the left and dark on the right, and a negative response where it is dark on the left and bright on the right.
After convolution, a ReLU replaces every negative value with 0 and keeps positives. This adds non-linearity without changing the map size (see activation functions).

Pooling shrinks each map. A 2×2 max-pooling window with stride 2 takes the largest value in each non-overlapping 2×2 block. Average pooling takes the mean instead. Pooling has no weights and no bias; it only has a window size and a stride. Its output size uses the same size formula.

blocks.where: n is the input side, f is the pooling window side, s is the pooling stride, p is padding (usually 0), and p_out is the pooled side.

blocks.text: For a 5×5 map with 2×2 pooling and stride 2: floor((5 − 2)/2) + 1 = 2, so the pooled map is 2×2. The four windows cover rows 1–2 and 3–4, and columns 1–2 and 3–4; row 5 and column 5 are dropped. Pooling lowers computation and gives small shift tolerance: if a feature moves by one pixel, it often stays inside the same window.

A CNN pipeline is: conv → ReLU → pool → (repeat conv-ReLU-pool) → flatten → dense → softmax. Flatten turns the final maps into one vector. Dense layers combine that vector, and softmax turns the final scores into class probabilities.

A CNN usually stacks several conv-ReLU-pool blocks. As depth increases, spatial size falls and the number of filters rises, so later layers see larger patterns with more channels. The final maps are flattened and passed to one or more dense layers.

items: LeNet-5: an early small CNN for handwritten digit recognition; convolution, pooling and dense layers.
AlexNet: a deeper CNN with ReLU and dropout that won the ImageNet image-classification challenge in 2012.
VGG: a simple design that repeats 3×3 convolutions in blocks; easy to describe but heavy in parameters.
ResNet: adds skip connections that let a signal bypass a block, so very deep networks train without the gradient vanishing.

blocks.text: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large dataset, such as ImageNet, and fine-tunes it on a small new dataset. The early conv filters often detect general edges and textures, so they transfer well.

figure.caption: Each row is one map, read left to right. The 3×3 filter turns the 5×5 input into the 3×3 conv map; its first value −4 is the worked dot product, ReLU zeroes the negatives, and 2×2 pooling with stride 1 gives 0 5 / 0 5.

spec.title: Worked example: filter, conv map, ReLU, pool
spec.aria: Four rows: the 3 by 3 filter 1 0 −1 repeated three times, the 3 by 3 convolution map −4 −1 5 −5 0 5 −4 −1 5, the ReLU map with all negatives set to zero, and the final 2 by 2 max-pooled map 0 5 0 5, each row read left to right as grid rows.

examples.question: A 5×5 single-channel image is given. A 3×3 filter is applied with stride 1 and no padding, then ReLU, then 2×2 max pooling with stride 1. (a) Find the convolution output size and the top-left convolution value. (b) Give the number of parameters in the convolution layer (one filter, with bias). (c) Give the final pooled 2×2 map. Input rows: 1 0 1 2 0 / 0 1 2 1 0 / 1 2 3 1 1 / 0 1 1 2 0 / 1 0 2 1 0. Filter rows: 1 0 −1 / 1 0 −1 / 1 0 −1.
steps: Input is 5×5 with one channel. Filter is 3×3: [[1,0,−1],[1,0,−1],[1,0,−1]].
Convolution output side = floor((5 + 2×0 − 3)/1) + 1 = 3. So the output map is 3×3.
Repeating for all 9 positions gives the convolution map: [[−4,−1,5],[−5,0,5],[−4,−1,5]].
ReLU keeps positives and sets negatives to 0: [[0,0,5],[0,0,5],[0,0,5]].
Pooling output side = floor((3 − 2)/1) + 1 = 2, so the pooled map is 2×2.
Four 2×2 windows with stride 1: top-left max(0,0,0,0)=0; top-right max(0,5,0,5)=5; bottom-left max(0,0,0,0)=0; bottom-right max(0,5,0,5)=5.
examples.answer: The convolution map is 3×3 with top-left value −4; the ReLU output feeds a 2×2 max pool with stride 1, giving [[0,5],[0,5]]; the conv layer has 10 parameters.

traps: Output size uses floor((n + 2p − f)/s) + 1. A 3×3 filter on a 5×5 input with stride 1 and no padding gives 3×3, not 5×5.
Pooling acts on the map it receives. A 3×3 convolution map pooled with a 2×2 window and stride 2 gives 1×1, not 2×2.
A filter's depth must equal the input channel count. Parameter count is f×f×C_in×K + K: use input channels, and add one bias per filter.
Pooling has no learnable weights or biases. Do not count pooling when the question asks for trainable parameters.
ReLU changes values but not shape. Flatten comes after the final pooling stage, before the dense layers, not before pooling.

quiz.q: What is a local receptive field in a convolution layer?
quiz.a: The small input patch (for example, 3×3) that one output value depends on. The filter sees only that patch at one position.

quiz.q: Why does weight sharing reduce the number of parameters?
quiz.a: The same filter weights are used at every position, so the parameter count depends on filter size, input channels and number of filters, not on the image size.

quiz.q: An input is 32×32×3. A convolution layer has 16 filters of size 3×3, stride 1 and padding 1. Find the output spatial size and the number of parameters (with bias).
quiz.a: Output side = floor((32 + 2 − 3)/1) + 1 = 32, so the output is 32×32×16. Parameters = 3×3×3×16 + 16 = 432 + 16 = 448.

quiz.q: A 4×4 map is passed through 2×2 max pooling with stride 2. Give the output size.
quiz.a: Pooled side = floor((4 − 2)/2) + 1 = 2, so the output is 2×2.

quiz.q: A 5×5 input goes through a 3×3 convolution (stride 1, no padding) and then 2×2 max pooling with stride 2. What is the pooled size? Why is it not 2×2?
quiz.a: The convolution gives 3×3. Pooling acts on that 3×3 map: floor((3 − 2)/2) + 1 = 1, so the pooled size is 1×1. It is not 2×2 because pooling does not see the original 5×5 input.

quiz.q: Why is max pooling partly tolerant to a small shift in the image?
quiz.a: A small shift moves a feature inside or near the same pooling window. Max pooling still picks the strongest response in that window, so the pooled value often changes little.

quiz.q: Name two pooling operations and one thing a pooling layer does not have.
quiz.a: Max pooling and average pooling. A pooling layer has no learnable weights or biases.

quiz.q: What does flatten do before a dense layer?
quiz.a: It converts the final 2D or 3D feature maps into one 1D vector so that dense-layer weights can multiply it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CNNs often replace a standard convolution with a depthwise separable convolution, which splits spatial filtering from channel mixing and cuts computation. Residual connections made very deep CNNs trainable, and transfer learning lets a model trained on millions of images be fine-tuned on a small local dataset. Newer vision transformers also patch images and attend across patches, but convolution remains the default for many embedded and mobile vision systems. Search for depthwise separable convolution, residual block, and ImageNet pre-trained models.
